spots.conservation_note: The south end of Catalina is a Marine Life Conservation District, a no-take reserve run by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.

spots.name: Little Eggs Beach
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. Parking in Avalon is metered and paid.
spots.parking_text: Paid metered parking in Avalon; street parking fills quickly in summer.
spots.hours_text: Beach open 24 hours. The Catalina Island Conservancy shuttle runs from Avalon.
spots.getting_there_text: From Avalon, take Pebble Beach Road about a mile and a half west to Little Eggs Beach, then a short sandy trail down to the water.
spots.depth_text: Rocky shore entry; the reef and kelp hold 6-20 ft
spots.best_season_text: Summer and early autumn, when the water is calmest and warmest.
spots.seasonal_warning: The north end of the beach is a protected cove for marine mammals and is closed to swimmers.
spots.hazards_text: A rough rock entry, kelp and marine life in the shallows, and swell. The Catalina Channel can build strong currents.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, 3/2 mm wetsuit, and water shoes for the rock entry.
spots.rules_text: No taking of marine life. Do not enter the closed marine mammal rookery at the north end. Stay on the trail and pack out everything.
spots.summary: A rocky Catalina cove at the islands west end, below a kelp forest and beside a protected marine mammal rookery.
highlights: A huge swell and a wild, remote feel
Kelp beds and rock in the shallows
A marine mammal rookery closed at the north end
spots.natural_features: Rocky lava shore, kelp forest and deep blue water off the exposed west end of Catalina.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm full suit, and a hood if you are staying out: the water runs 60-65F (16-18C) and the wind picks up in the afternoon.
spots.water_temp_note: 60-68F (16-20C), with the biggest swell from November to March.
rules_do: Watch the swell before you enter, because it runs hard here
Stay on the trail and keep clear of the rookery fence
Go with a buddy: the current can build quickly
rules_avoid: Do not enter the closed marine mammal rookery
Do not take marine life
Do not swim past the point alone
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: deep-water frogfish, deepwater frogfish, spiny-head anglerfish, 黑紋裸身躄魚, 黑纹裸身躄鱼 by Kai Squires · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The whole south end of Catalina is a Marine Life Conservation District, and Little Eggs has an additional seasonal closure around the sea lion and seal rookery.

spots.name: Sunset Cliffs Marine Reserve
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. Parking at the La Jolla Farms lot north of the bluffs is paid.
spots.parking_text: Paid parking at the La Jolla Farms lot and along Sunset Cliffs Boulevard. Street parking is scarce.
spots.getting_there_text: South of the Scripps Pier, along Sunset Cliffs Boulevard in Ocean Beach.
spots.depth_text: Rocky shore entry with reef ledges out to about 15 ft
spots.best_season_text: Summer for the kelp forest. A winter swell is common. Mornings are calmest.
spots.seasonal_warning: Swell surges into the caves and surge channels, so go with a guide if you are not confident in a rocky entry.
spots.hazards_text: Rocky entry, heavy surf and rip currents. This is a snorkel-and-dive site, not a swim beach.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A 3/2 mm wetsuit and booties are normal here.
spots.rules_text: No taking of marine life inside the reserve. Do not walk on the kelp or the rock. Keep a wide berth from seals and sea lions.
spots.summary: A rocky marine reserve under the Sunset Cliffs bluffs where the kelp forest comes right to the shore.
highlights: A kelp forest under the bluffs
Rock and sand shelves full of fish
Sea lions on the rocks near the beach
spots.natural_features: Rocky shore and a sheltered kelp forest, with sand channels and a rocky reef under the sandstone cliffs.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm full suit: the water runs 62-67F (16-19C), and it is warmer in the kelp but colder in the open.
spots.water_temp_note: 62-70F (16-21C), coldest in February and March.
rules_do: Enter from the rocks at the north end, where the surge is gentler
Keep a wide berth from the seals and sea lions on the beach
Go in the morning, when the surf is smallest
rules_avoid: Do not take marine life inside the reserve
Do not walk on the kelp or the rock
Do not swim in a rip current
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: File:Monte Rio Theater, Near the California Coast (5378916919).jpg by Tony Fischer · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The reserve was created in 1972 and covers the kelp forest and rocky habitat under the Sunset Cliffs bluffs, with no take and no anchoring in the kelp.

spots.name: Scripps Pier
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. The pier is open to the public.
spots.parking_text: Paid parking in the Scripps Institution lot and along the street.
spots.hours_text: The pier is open from sunrise to sunset.
spots.getting_there_text: Off La Jolla Scenic Drive in La Jolla, next to the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.
spots.depth_text: The pier stands over about 12 ft of water; the reef below drops to 40 ft
spots.best_season_text: Best near high tide. The tidewalk runs for roughly two hours before and after high tide.
spots.seasonal_warning: The water is often green with plankton and visibility can be poor on windy days.
spots.hazards_text: Strong rip currents run around the pier pilings. Never swim off the Scripps pier, and note there is no lifeguard on the pier itself.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A 3/2 mm wetsuit most of the year. Scripps publishes a tidewalk species guide.
spots.protected_area_name: Scripps Institution of Oceanography Marine Reserve
spots.rules_text: Do not touch the pier pilings or the marine life on them. It is illegal to take any marine life. Stay inside the posted swim zone.
spots.summary: A public research pier in La Jolla with a summer tidewalk program and a deep reef just below the pilings.
highlights: A kelp bed and tidepool reef just below the pier pilings
Leopard sharks in the summer shallows
A working pier with pelicans and sea lions on it
spots.natural_features: Rocky reef and kelp in the shallows, with the pilings of the pier covered in marine growth.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from June to September, when the water is 64-68F (18-20C). A full suit in the winter.
spots.water_temp_note: 63-69F (17-21C), coldest in February and warmest in September.
rules_do: Snorkel at high tide, when the tidewalk runs for about two hours either side of it
Stay in the posted swim zone, which is watched by lifeguards
Shuffle your feet in the sand for stingrays
rules_avoid: Do not swim off the pier: rips run around the pilings
Do not touch the pilings or the life on them
Do not take any marine life

spots.conservation_note: The reef under the pier is a Marine Life Conservation District, and Scripps Institution of Oceanography runs long-term monitoring of the leopard shark aggregation in the summer.

spots.name: Manatee Springs State Park
spots.entry_fee_text: Free.
spots.parking_text: Free parking at the park. There is a small lot at the spring and a larger one at the headwaters.
spots.getting_there_text: Off US 19 at Manatee Springs Road, near Chiefland.
spots.depth_text: Shallow. The spring pool is about 4-5 ft deep and the river run is knee to waist deep.
spots.best_season_text: Best on a weekday morning, year-round. The water is about 68-70 degrees.
spots.hazards_text: The river can be deep in places. Do not get in the water directly over the spring head: a floating person can be pulled down.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, a shorty in winter.
spots.rules_text: Do not swim directly over the spring head. Do not feed or touch manatees; keep your distance and never approach a calf. No glass containers.
spots.summary: A clear shallow spring where wild manatees gather in the cooler months and the river runs green with duckweed.
highlights: Wild manatees in the cooler months
A clear spring pool about 70F all year
A river run lined with cypress and a big spring head
spots.natural_features: A limestone spring head discharging into a clear, deep river run, with a boardwalk and an open viewing area.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: No wetsuit. The water holds 68-70F (20-21C) all year, so it is a swimsuit rather than a wetsuit day.
spots.water_temp_note: 68-70F (20-21C) year-round, and clearest in the early morning before wind picks up.
rules_do: Watch from the boardwalk before you get in the water
Stay out of the spring head area, where a floating person can be pulled down
Use a float in the river run
rules_avoid: Do not feed or touch manatees, and never approach a calf

spots.conservation_note: Manatee Springs hosts one of the largest concentrations of manatees in Florida, and the state runs a tag-and-release study here through the Florida Fish and Wildlife Research Institute.

spots.name: Fanning Springs State Park
spots.entry_fee_text: $6 per vehicle or per person.
spots.parking_text: Free parking inside the park entrance.
spots.getting_there_text: At the end of Fanning Springs Road, off US 19 near Chiefland.
spots.depth_text: The spring bowl is 6-18 ft deep; the river runs away from it in a strong, cold current.
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. The water is 72 degrees, and manatees are more likely in the cooler months.
spots.hazards_text: A very strong current runs out of the spring and into the river, and swimming against it is exhausting. There is no lifeguard.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, a rash guard or shorty. A float is a good idea because of the current.
spots.rules_text: Do not swim in the spring bowl itself: it is a protected area and the current there is dangerous. Stay in the river and keep clear of the spring head.
spots.summary: One of Floridas largest springs, pouring 65 million gallons a day into a strong cold river that manatees use.
highlights: A clear 72F spring run you can swim for a mile
Manatees that gather in the cooler months
A deep spring bowl fed by 65 million gallons a day
spots.natural_features: A limestone spring that discharges into the Suwannee River, with a deep bowl, a shaded river run and cypress and oak on the banks.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: No wetsuit. The water holds 72F (22C) all year. If you are cold-sensitive, bring a 1mm suit.
spots.water_temp_note: 68-72F (20-22C) all year, because the water comes from the aquifer and never sees sunlight.
rules_do: Use a float and a snorkel in the river run
Keep to the river and stay clear of the spring head
Swim with the current on the way out and against nothing on the way back
rules_avoid: Do not swim in the spring bowl: it is protected and the current is dangerous
Do not feed or touch manatees
Do not bring glass into the water
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Seagrass Zostera marina (Dzharylhach island) by Sofia Sadogurska · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Fanning Springs is one of the largest springs in the world by discharge, and its manatee population is monitored by the FWC and by Georgia State University research crews.

spots.name: Gilchrist Blue Springs
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. There is no entrance fee and no parking fee.
spots.parking_text: Free gravel parking lot beside the spring.
spots.getting_there_text: Off County Road 340 in High Springs, about two miles west of town.
spots.depth_text: Shallow, 2-4 ft for most of the run; the spring pool is about 12 ft deep.
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. The water is 68-70 degrees.
spots.seasonal_warning: The river current can pick up quickly after rain. Stay out of the main channel and do not swim upstream of the spring pool.
spots.hazards_text: Visibility drops after heavy rain, and the pool has a steep drop-off on the upstream side.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A shorty or a 3 mm suit in winter.
spots.rules_text: Do not swim above the spring pool where the current is strong. Do not take shells or any marine life. No glass.
spots.summary: A shallow, swimmable blue spring that runs about a quarter of a mile to the Santa Fe River.
highlights: A short, clear swim in 68-70F water
A spring run that leads straight to the Santa Fe River
Turtles, fish and cypress shaded water
spots.natural_features: A limestone spring with a deep pool at the head, a short run and the Santa Fe River 200 yards downstream.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: No wetsuit. The water holds 68-70F (20-21C) all year.
spots.water_temp_note: 68-70F (20-21C) year-round. Visibility drops sharply after heavy rain, which brings tannin into the run.
rules_do: Swim the run rather than the pool, where the current is stronger
Park in the free lot and walk in
Go on a weekday, when the pool is quiet
rules_avoid: Do not swim above the spring pool, where the current is strong
Do not take shells or any marine life
Do not bring glass
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: An underwater scene from an aquarium featuring small, colorful fish swimming in a sandy... by Faisal Ahammad · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Gilchrist Blue Springs is part of the Gilchrist County Springs system, and the Santa Fe River below it is a Wild and Scenic River with its own protection.

spots.name: Rainbow Springs State Park
spots.entry_fee_text: $8 per vehicle, or $6 per person if you enter on foot or by bike.
spots.parking_text: Parking at the park entrance. A boardwalk runs to the head spring pool.
spots.getting_there_text: Off US 19 at Rainbow Springs, about 10 miles north of Dunnellon.
spots.depth_text: The main pool is 5-18 ft deep; the cave is about 400 ft long and 2-6 ft deep.
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. The water holds 72 degrees all year, so winter is the best value.
spots.hazards_text: Glass-clear water with very low visibility beyond a few feet. Do not dive into the cave. There is no lifeguard.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, a rash guard, and a light if you want to see into the cave. A shorty or no suit works year-round in 72 degree water.
spots.rules_text: Do not enter the cave - it is closed to swimmers. Do not swim in the river above the spring. Glass containers are prohibited.
spots.summary: A cold 72 degree spring pool and a 400-foot swimming cave at the head of the Rainbow River.
highlights: A 5 to 18 ft deep spring pool at 72F all year
A 400 ft cave you cannot swim into
A white sand bottom in water you can see across
spots.natural_features: A karst spring with a deep, clear pool, a white sand bottom and a collapse cave beside it, fed by the Floridan aquifer.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: No wetsuit. The water holds 72F (22C) all year, so it is comfortable for swimming in summer and winter alike.
spots.water_temp_note: 68-72F (20-22C) all year, with the clearest water in the early morning.
rules_do: Snorkel the pool rather than the cave, which is closed to swimmers
Wear shoes for the walk down, because the path is rough
Go on a weekday, when the crowd is smaller
rules_avoid: Do not enter the cave
Do not swim in the river above the spring
Do not bring glass into the water
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: A variety of bright yellow and orange tropical fish swim together in a clear blue aquar... by Faisal Ahammad · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Rainbow Springs is one of the largest first-magnitude springs in Florida, and its cave and pool are habitat for the Florida cave crayfish and for the green turtle population that uses the spring run.

spots.name: Sand Key Lighthouse
spots.area_label: Sand Key, west of Key West
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. The islet is reached by water taxi; the fare varies by operator.
spots.parking_text: There is no parking on the islet. Water taxis leave from the Old Town Key West docks.
spots.hours_text: Accessible when the water allows. The islet has no services.
spots.getting_there_text: Water taxi or private boat from Key West, about eight miles out.
spots.depth_text: The lighthouse base and the surrounding reef are 5-15 ft
spots.best_season_text: Summer for calm water and clear visibility.
spots.seasonal_warning: Boat passage to the islet can be cancelled in rough weather.
spots.hazards_text: The trip out is open water with heavy boat traffic, and the islet has no shade and no freshwater.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, a dive flag, sun protection and water.
spots.protected_area_type: Historic lighthouse (National Register) on a natural reef
spots.rules_text: Do not take marine life. Stay off the reef and do not touch the historic lighthouse. Carry a dive flag.
spots.summary: A red-and-white lighthouse on a sand islet eight miles west of Key West, ringed by shallow reef.
highlights: A historic lighthouse on a tiny sand island
Shallow reef with good fish life
Almost no one else on the water
spots.natural_features: A low sand islet with a shallow reef platform around it, a rock breakwater and a coral head on the south side.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A rash guard. The water is 78-85F (26-29C) in summer and 73-76F (23-24C) in winter.
spots.water_temp_note: 73-85F (23-29C), with the calmest water and the clearest visibility in summer.
rules_do: Carry a dive flag
Take water and sun protection, because the islet has no shade and no freshwater
Stay clear of the surf line around the sand
rules_avoid: Do not take marine life
Do not touch the historic lighthouse
Do not stand on the reef
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: A serene beach scene with clear blue skies and turquoise water. A red and white jet ski... by Nasim Miah · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Sand Key Light has been on the National Register of Historic Places since 1989, and the islet and its surrounding reef sit inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary.

spots.name: Old Seven Mile Bridge Piles
spots.entry_fee_text: Free.
spots.parking_text: Free parking at the Old Seven Mile Bridge parking area on US 1 in Marathon.
spots.getting_there_text: On US 1 in Marathon, at the west end of the Old Seven Mile Bridge, at the historic bridge parking area.
spots.depth_text: Shallow, about 3-6 ft over the old bridge pilings
spots.best_season_text: Year-round, best on a calm day.
spots.hazards_text: The remains of the old bridge are shallow, barnacle-covered and sharp. Stay clear of the current bridge piers.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. Water shoes for the barnacles.
spots.protected_area_type: Historic highway bridge remains (Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary)
spots.rules_text: Do not take anything from the structure and do not cut or loosen barnacles. Do not dive under the current bridge piers.
spots.summary: The stumps of the old 1912 Overseas Railway bridge, a shallow historic snorkel in the middle of Marathon.
highlights: Concrete bridge stumps standing in clear water
Barnacles and coral growth on the old piers
A heritage trail on the new bridge above you
spots.natural_features: The concrete stumps and cutwaters of the 1912 Overseas Railway bridge, standing in shallow water on a sand and rubble bottom.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A rash guard. The water is 74-84F (23-29C) in summer and 72-76F (22-24C) in winter.
spots.water_temp_note: 72-84F (22-29C), and the water is clearest in the winter.
rules_do: Keep clear of the current bridge piers and never dive under them
Stay on the outer face of the stumps, where the current is lighter
Bring a mask that will not leak, because the structure is jagged
rules_avoid: Do not take anything from the structure
Do not cut or loosen barnacles
Do not touch the new bridge piers
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: That S The Spot by Tilonaut · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The old bridge is part of the Overseas Railroad Heritage Trail and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary protects the structure and the marine life growing on it.

spots.name: Dry Tortugas National Park
spots.entry_fee_text: The park entrance fee is $15 per person; children under 16 enter free. Boat passage is extra and varies by operator.
spots.reservation_text: A park entrance permit is required, and ferry or boat passage should be booked in advance in high season.
spots.parking_text: There is no parking on the island. Everything comes in by ferry or boat.
spots.hours_text: The park is open 24 hours. The ferry runs from Key West, and the trip takes about two hours.
spots.getting_there_text: Ferry from Key West, or a boat from Key West, Marathon or Key Largo.
spots.depth_text: The moat wall and reef top are 5-20 ft, with drop-offs of 50-100 ft
spots.best_season_text: The island is visitable year-round, but the water is usually calmest in summer.
spots.seasonal_warning: There is no freshwater and almost no shade on the island. Boat passage can be cancelled in rough weather.
spots.hazards_text: Heat, sun exposure and dehydration are the real dangers here. The moat wall has heavy surge and the reef drop-offs come up fast.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, a dive flag, serious sun protection and at least a gallon of water per person.
spots.rules_text: National park rules apply: no collecting of marine life or coral, no touching the fort walls or artefacts, a dive flag is required, and a permit is needed to moor a boat overnight.
spots.summary: The largest tropical dry island reserve in the United States, 70 miles beyond Key West, with a third of the worlds coral reef systems.
highlights: The clearest water in the continental United States
The intact coral of the Florida reef, with drop-offs
More than 300 wrecks, and an 1800s brick fort
spots.natural_features: The Florida reef at its most intact: coral, spur-and-groove and a reef wall that drops into deep blue water.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from November to March. The water is 72-76F (22-24C) in winter and 84-88F (29-31C) in summer, and there is no shade for hours.
spots.water_temp_note: 72-88F (22-31C). The season does not change the water temperature much; it changes the swell.
rules_do: Fly a dive flag
Carry at least a gallon of water per person and use the shade on the island
Stay on the marked trails and off the fort walls
rules_avoid: Do not collect marine life or coral
Do not touch the fort walls or any artefact
Do not swim in the moat: American crocodiles live there
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Underwater Scene by Robert Caney · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Dry Tortugas became a national park in 1937 and its waters are a marine sanctuary. The fort and the wrecks are protected as cultural resources, and the American crocodile population here is one of the northernmost in the range.

spots.name: John Pennekamp State Park
alt_names: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
spots.entry_fee_text: Free to enter the park. The glass-bottom boat is priced separately, at roughly $30-35 per adult.
spots.reservation_text: A reservation is strongly recommended for the glass-bottom boat; walk-up seats are released if the boat is not full.
spots.parking_text: Park parking is free and fills early at weekends.
spots.hours_text: The park is open daily. The glass-bottom boat normally runs a morning and an afternoon departure.
spots.getting_there_text: On US 1 in Key Largo, about 60 miles north of Key West and 25 miles south of Marathon.
spots.depth_text: The reef top is 10-20 ft in the shallow area and drops to 60-100 ft along the wall
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. The clearest water is usually in summer.
spots.hazards_text: A dive flag is required by state law for snorkelers and divers in the park, and the current runs hard along the reef edge.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins, and a dive flag. The boat provides both the flag and the guide.
spots.protected_area_name: John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park
spots.protected_area_type: State park / Marine Life Conservation District
spots.rules_text: Spearfishing is prohibited. Do not take coral or marine life. A dive flag is required, and you must stay on the marked snorkel trail.
spots.summary: The first undersea park in the world, where the reef starts at the beach and runs 21 miles to the edge of the shelf.
highlights: The reef that starts right at the sand
Coral heads, turtles and the clearest water in the Keys
A glass-bottom boat trip if you would rather stay dry
spots.natural_features: The Florida reef at its northern start point: hardbottom, coral heads and a spur-and-groove reef that runs parallel to the shore.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from November to March, when the water is 72-76F (22-24C). A rash guide in summer.
spots.water_temp_note: 73-85F (23-29C), with the clearest water in late summer and early autumn.
rules_do: Fly a dive flag: it is required by state law for snorkelers as well as divers
Stay on the marked snorkel trail
Take a towel and a cover-up, because the boat ride is as much of the day as the snorkel
rules_avoid: Do not spearfish anywhere in the park
Do not take coral or marine life
Do not swim outside the marked snorkel trail
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Coral Reef aerial by Photo courtesy of Sean Connolly. · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The park was created in 1959 as the world's first undersea park, and the reef tract it protects runs about 21 miles out to the edge of the continental shelf.

spots.name: SS Copenhagen
spots.entry_fee_text: Free to dive the site; boat operators charge for the trip.
spots.reservation_text: Boat operators require a diver log sheet and proof of certification.
spots.parking_text: Not applicable - boat access only.
spots.hours_text: Boat operators schedule around the swell; calm weekday mornings are best.
spots.getting_there_text: Charter dive boats leave from Lauderdale-by-the-Sea and from the Hillsboro Beach and Pompano docks.
spots.depth_text: The top of the wreck sits in about 25 ft of water.
spots.best_season_text: Year-round on calm days. Visibility is usually best in summer.
spots.seasonal_warning: This is a dive site rather than a snorkel site: the wreck lies well below snorkel depth and it is a protected historic site.
spots.hazards_text: Currents at the site are mild, but the site sits outside the protected swim zone and boat traffic is heavy.
spots.gear_text: Scuba gear and a dive computer. This site is for divers, not snorkelers.
spots.rules_text: No touching, no artefact removal and no change to the site. This is a state-designated underwater archaeological preserve: spearfishing and any form of take are prohibited.
spots.summary: A British steamship that wrecked in May 1900 less than a mile offshore, now a protected historic dive site.
highlights: The most intact wooden wreck in Florida waters
Large coral growth on the hull and the debris field
Sargassum, barracuda and large fish in open water
spots.natural_features: A deep-water debris field with the wooden hull of a ship broken in two, covered in hardbottom coral growth, in open coastal water.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm full suit, and this is a dive site rather than a snorkel site: the wreck sits in about 25 ft of water.
spots.water_temp_note: 72-84F (22-29C), with visibility usually best in summer.
rules_do: Watch for boat traffic: the site sits outside the protected swim zone
Stay on the surface on the first dive and find the site from there
Fly a dive flag
rules_avoid: Do not touch, do not move and do not remove anything
Do not spearfish: it is prohibited inside the preserve
Do not enter the protected zone from the surface without a boat
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Coron Island, Palawan, Philippines 1 by Ray in Manila · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The SS Copenhagen was declared a Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve in 1994. Within a preserve it is unlawful to damage, remove or alter the site, which is why the coral on the wreck is one of the oldest measured on a Florida shipwreck.

spots.name: Shipwreck Snorkel Trail
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. The snorkel trail is open to the public.
spots.parking_text: Paid metered parking on El Mar Drive and on A1A.
spots.hours_text: Open 24 hours. Anglins Pier itself is closed for reconstruction until roughly 2028.
spots.getting_there_text: Swim in from the Datura Avenue beach portal, or enter from the sand east of the pier.
spots.depth_text: 10 ft of water over the trail
spots.best_season_text: Year-round, on a calm day with low swell.
spots.seasonal_warning: The trail markers are small pairs of yellow buoys and are easy to miss from the surface.
spots.hazards_text: Boat traffic is the main risk. The pier is closed for reconstruction, so there is construction activity around the shoreline.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A dive flag if you have one. The trail runs over a rocky, weedy bottom.
spots.rules_text: No taking of marine life or artefacts. Do not touch the wreck structures, the cannon or the anchor. Yield to boats and never enter the marked channel.
spots.summary: A 2002 snorkel trail over a British steamship broken up in the 1970s, dedicated by Jean-Michele Cousteau.
highlights: The anchor, five cannon and a ballast pile at 10 ft
Yellow marker buoys that lead you along the trail
Clear water over a flat rubble bottom
spots.natural_features: A man-made snorkel trail over the debris field of the SS Copenhagen, on a flat rubble and sand bottom with low relief coral.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from November to March, when the water is 72-75F (22-24C). Most people snorkel without one in summer.
spots.water_temp_note: 72-84F (22-29C), with the clearest water in winter.
rules_do: Follow the paired yellow marker buoys and stay with them
Keep to the shallow bottom and do not dive below the trail
Give way to boats and stay clear of the marked channel
rules_avoid: Do not touch the wreck pieces, the cannon or the anchor
Do not take any artefact or marine life
Do not snorkel in the marked channel
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: An underwater scene showing a sea turtle and several tropical fish swimming around a mo... by Faisal Ahammad · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The trail was dedicated in 2002 by Jean-Michele Cousteau with the Marine Archaeological Council, a nonprofit he inspired to protect Florida shipwrecks. The site sits next to the Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve of the SS Copenhagen.

spots.name: Datura Avenue Reef
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. Street access to a public beach; parking on Datura Avenue is metered and paid.
spots.parking_text: Paid metered parking along Datura Avenue and in the municipal lot on El Mar Drive. The town also has a vehicle rack for bikes and boards.
spots.hours_text: The beach portal is open 24 hours.
spots.getting_there_text: On Datura Avenue at El Mar Drive, one block east of the beach in Lauderdale-by-the-Sea.
spots.depth_text: Waist to chest deep over a natural reef shelf; sand bottom inside
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. Calmest on a weekday morning, and the reef is close enough to shore to snorkel in almost any conditions.
spots.hazards_text: This is a street-access beach with no lifeguard. Watch for boat traffic and stay clear of the pier and the channel.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A rash guard, and a shorty in winter. The reef is close to shore so a snorkel alone is enough.
spots.protected_area_type: Broward County nearshore hardbottom and rubble reef
spots.rules_text: No taking of marine life. Do not stand on the coral. This is a boat-staging area: give way to divers and never snorkel in the marked channel.
spots.summary: A three-tier natural reef that starts about 100 yards off a street-end beach portal in Lauderdale-by-the-Sea.
highlights: A three-tier natural reef that starts about 100 yards from the beach
Turtles and schooling fish on the first terrace
A reef you can snorkel without ever getting on a boat
spots.natural_features: A living hardbottom reef that steps down in three terraces, with spur-and-groove coral and sand channels between them.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from November to March (72-75F / 22-24C). Most people snorkel without one in summer.
spots.water_temp_note: 72-85F (22-29C), with the clearest water in winter and the warmest in August.
rules_do: Look for the beach portal at the end of Datura Avenue and swim out on the bearing of the markers
Watch for boat traffic and stay out of the channel
Stay on the first terrace if you are not confident in open water
rules_avoid: Do not stand on the coral
Do not take any marine life
Do not snorkel in the marked channel: it is a boat staging area
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Coral reef and colorful fish from an aquarium by mdburnette · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The reef sits inside the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary boundary at its northern edge, and the marine archaeological preserve offshore adds a second layer of protection.

spots.name: Crandon Park
spots.entry_fee_text: Free. Parking is paid, but the City of Miami Beach issues free three-hour parking passes.
spots.parking_text: Paid metered parking in the Crandon Park lot. The city provides free three-hour parking passes at parking meters.
spots.getting_there_text: Across the bridge from Miami Beach on Crandon Boulevard, about 20 minutes from South Beach.
spots.depth_text: Sandy bottom; shallow reef patches in places; no drop-off
spots.best_season_text: Year-round. Mornings are calmest and the water is clearest in winter.
spots.hazards_text: The shoreline stays shallow for a long way out, which makes this a good beginner beach. Watch the boat channel markers and stay on the ocean side.
spots.gear_text: Mask, snorkel and fins. A rash guard in summer, a shorty in winter.
spots.rules_text: Do not take shells or coral. No glass containers. Do not feed the fish. Obey the lifeguard flags.
spots.summary: A wide sandy beach and park on Key Biscayne, with an easy shallow swim and a low reef on the north end.
highlights: A sandy bottom that stays shallow for a long way out
Stingrays in the shallows and a small reef at the north end
Birds and a wide, uncrowded beach at the south end
spots.natural_features: Sand and seagrass flats with a nearshore patch reef at the north end of the beach.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A rash guard most of the year. A 3mm shorty for December to March, when the water is 72-75F (22-24C).
spots.water_temp_note: 72-84F (22-29C), with the clearest water and the biggest swell in winter.
rules_do: Stay on the ocean side of the channel markers
Walk on the sand and shuffle your feet for stingrays
Use the free three-hour parking passes from the City of Miami Beach
rules_avoid: Do not take shells or coral
Do not feed the fish
Do not bring glass containers
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: Sandkey by No machine-readable author provided. Drdisque assumed (based on copyright claims). · CC BY (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: Crandon sits on Key Biscayne, which was the site of the Miami Marine Stadium and is now part of the Crandon Park and Beach natural area, with turtle nesting monitored on the north end.

spots.name: La Jolla Shores (Leopard Sharks)
spots.entry_fee_text: Free
spots.parking_text: Free lot at Kellogg Park fills early in summer; street parking nearby.
spots.getting_there_text: At the south end of La Jolla Shores beach, in front of the Marine Room.
spots.depth_text: Shallow sandy flats
spots.best_season_text: Summer, when leopard sharks gather in the warm shallows.
spots.hazards_text: Shore break at the waterline. Shuffle your feet for stingrays.
spots.rules_text: No taking of marine life. Keep your distance; never touch the sharks.
spots.summary: Harmless leopard sharks gather over the sand in summer at the south end of La Jolla Shores, an easy beach entry.
highlights: Leopard sharks in the shallow sand from June to October
A student kelp bed protected by a marine reserve
A calm, shallow shore that beginners can use
spots.natural_features: A sand and cobble beach with a rocky kelp bed just offshore, and a protected student reserve on the reef.
spots.wetsuit_recommendation: A 3mm shorty from June to September, when the water is 64-68F (18-20C). A full suit is more comfortable in the winter.
spots.water_temp_note: 63-69F (17-21C), coldest in February, warmest in September.
rules_do: Shuffle your feet when you walk on the sand: stingrays bury themselves there
Keep 10 ft (3 m) from the leopard sharks and never touch them
Snorkel in the marked swim zone at Scripps
rules_avoid: Do not take any marine life
Do not touch or stand on the kelp bed
Do not swim off the pier, where rips run around the pilings
spots.hero_image_credit: Photo: leopardhai, leopardhaj, leopardihai, leopard-nugishai, leopard shark, luipaardhaai, pru... by Jonathan Whitaker · CC0 (cropped and colour-graded)
spots.conservation_note: The kelp bed off La Jolla Shores is a Marine Life Conservation District, and the leopard sharks there are a protected species that is routinely monitored by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

species.protection_text: Protected under the US Endangered Species Act.
species.distance_rule: Stay at least 10 ft (3 m) away. Never touch, chase or block its path to the surface.
species.description: Grazes on algae and seagrass close to shore; often rests on the reef or visits fish cleaning stations.

species.protection_text: Endangered; one of the rarest seals in the world.
species.distance_rule: Stay at least 50 ft (15 m) away, and 150 ft (45 m) from a mother and pup.
species.description: Hauls out on beaches to rest. Resting seals are not stranded; leave them be.

species.protection_text: Protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act.
species.distance_rule: In Hawaii it is illegal to approach within 50 yards (46 m).
species.description: Rests in shallow bays by day and feeds offshore at night.

species.protection_text: Protected from take in Hawaii.
species.distance_rule: Float at the surface and keep your hands to yourself; let the manta come to you.
species.description: Filter-feeds on plankton; in Kona it visits lights set out at night.
Hawaii's state fish, common on shallow reef flats.
Bright yellow surgeonfish that grazes algae in schools.
Crunches dead coral and turns it into sand; listen for it.
Striped reef fish with a long trailing dorsal fin.

species.protection_text: California's state marine fish; protected from take.
species.description: Bright orange damselfish that guards its patch of rocky reef.

species.distance_rule: Harmless and shy. Watch from above; never touch or chase.
species.description: Gathers in warm, sandy shallows off La Jolla Shores in summer.

species.protection_text: Protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act.
species.distance_rule: Give at least 50 ft (15 m); never approach resting animals on rocks.
species.description: Rests on the cliffs and rocks around La Jolla and Catalina.
Small, slow bottom-dwelling shark that hides in rocky crevices by day.
Common predator in kelp forests.
Fast-growing brown algae that forms underwater forests along the California coast.

species.protection_text: Federally threatened.
species.distance_rule: Passive observation only: no touching, chasing or feeding.
species.description: Slow-moving grazer of seagrass in warm, shallow water.

species.distance_rule: Usually rests on the bottom; do not touch or corner it.
species.description: Bottom-dwelling shark often seen resting under ledges.

species.distance_rule: Shuffle your feet when wading over sand.
species.description: Rests half-buried in sand flats.

species.protection_text: Protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act.
species.distance_rule: Never feed or swim toward dolphins.
species.description: Often seen from boats in Biscayne Bay.

species.protection_text: Threatened under the US Endangered Species Act.
species.distance_rule: Never stand on, touch or kick coral.
species.description: Branching reef-building coral, focus of Florida restoration programs.
Disc-shaped fish that cruises in schools over reefs and wrecks.

species.protection_text: Not protected in Florida, but never take one. Many are already gone from the reef.
species.distance_rule: Stay about three feet away and let it graze in peace.
species.description: One of the most recognisable reef fish in the Caribbean, with blue-edged yellow scales and a bright orange patch over the eye. You will usually meet them in pairs.

species.protection_text: Protected as a coral reef fish. Taking one is a federal offence.
species.distance_rule: Give them a wide berth; they are often asleep under an overhang.
species.description: The most common large parrotfish on Florida reefs. Adults can change colour from red to green to yellow and are usually seen grazing algae off the reef.

species.protection_text: Protected as a coral reef fish. Do not take.
species.distance_rule: Keep a respectful distance and never touch the tail or the sharp spine at the base of it.
species.description: Electric blue with a black marking and a yellow tail. Adults can be territorial toward other blue tangs, so watch which one you are approaching.

species.protection_text: Protected as a coral reef fish and regulated by size limits in Florida waters.
species.distance_rule: Do not spear or touch a spawning aggregation.
species.description: A silvery snapper with a bright yellow stripe. They hang in loose groups above the reef and are easiest to see near drop-offs.

species.protection_text: Protected as a coral reef fish.
species.distance_rule: Keep your hands to yourself around the schools; they hang over coral heads.
species.description: Yellow and silver with narrow bronze stripes. Big schools hang motionless above patch reefs in the Keys and on the upper shelf.

species.protection_text: Protected. Never dig a jawfish out of its burrow.
species.distance_rule: Stay a foot away from the burrow and never block its entrance.
species.description: It lives in a burrow in the sand and pops its head out to look at you. It will not tolerate a hand near the hole and may abandon it.

species.protection_text: Protected as a migratory species in Florida waters.
species.distance_rule: Never chase or touch one; they are agile and a tail strike can hurt.
species.description: Dark wings with white spots and a long whip tail. They cruise the sandy channels and are often visible from the surface at the edge of the reef.

species.protection_text: Highly regulated; federal and state sport-fishing rules apply.
species.distance_rule: Keep well clear of the bill. Never swim toward a sailfish.
species.description: The fastest fish in the ocean. Offshore of the Keys you will see the tall dorsal fin cutting the surface long before you see the fish.

species.protection_text: Protected as a coral reef fish in Florida.
species.distance_rule: Do not chase a barracuda; they are curious but they are predators.
species.description: A long silver fish that hangs motionless over the reef, usually with a few smaller fish travelling alongside it.

species.protection_text: Endangered under both federal and Florida law.
species.distance_rule: Do not approach. Keep at least ten feet and never block its path to the surface.
species.description: A smaller sea turtle with a narrow, hooked beak and a beautifully patterned shell. A handful still nest on the Florida Keys beaches.

species.protection_text: Threatened under federal law and protected in Florida.
species.distance_rule: Ten feet away, and never between a turtle and the water.
species.description: The most common sea turtle on Florida beaches, with a big blocky head and reddish-brown shell. It nests in high numbers along the Atlantic coast and the Keys.

species.protection_text: Protected; there is a recreational bag limit and a closed season in some waters.
species.distance_rule: Never lift a lobster off the reef by the tail - take it by the carapace.
species.description: No big claws, just long antennae. They hide in crevices by day and come out to feed at night.

species.protection_text: Not protected, but never take it.
species.distance_rule: Watch from a distance; they wave their long white antennae when they sense you.
species.description: Cleaner shrimp that set up cleaning stations on the reef, picking parasites off fish and even cleaning the mouth of a passing diver.

species.protection_text: Protected. Coral and all, a sea fan is a living colony you cannot replace.
species.distance_rule: Do not touch, and give the fan a wide berth so the current does not break it.
species.description: A flat, fan-shaped colony that grows across the current. On a good reef you can see dozens of them, each one a tiny city of polyps.

species.protection_text: Not protected in Florida, but never handle one.
species.distance_rule: Do not pick it up; it can release sticky Cuvier tubules.
species.description: A soft brown sausage-shaped animal that walks slowly over the sand and reef, filtering sand for food.

species.protection_text: Endangered in Florida under the Endangered Species Act and the Coral Reef Protection Act.
species.distance_rule: Never touch, stand on or break a branch. It can take decades to grow back.
species.description: The fast-growing branching coral that once covered much of Floridas shallow reef. It was hit by disease and hurricanes and is now being grown in nurseries and replanted.

species.protection_text: Not protected, but a state sport fish with strict catch limits.
species.distance_rule: Keep a fish in the water alive if you hook one.
species.description: The green bass of Floridas clear springs and rivers. In the springs they gather under the lily pads in cold water, which concentrates them.

species.protection_text: Not protected, but a state sport fish with a protected slot limit.
species.distance_rule: Keep it in the water and do not take a fish you cannot identify.
species.description: A prehistoric-looking predator with a long dorsal fin, living in the quiet back waters of Florida springs and rivers.

species.protection_text: Not protected.
species.distance_rule: Handle with care; the jaw is strong and the teeth are sharp.
species.description: A long, armoured fish with a rounded snout that hangs motionless in the weed beds of the springs.

species.protection_text: Not protected, but never take it.
species.distance_rule: Watch them flicking in the seagrass; do not disturb the meadow.
species.description: Tiny transparent shrimp that flicker in and out of the seagrass and are the first thing you notice when you float over a grass bed.

experiences.name: Guided sea turtle walk at Juno Beach
experiences.description: Permitted night walk on one of the densest loggerhead nesting beaches in the world, after a talk at the sea turtle hospital. Sightings are not guaranteed.
experiences.donation_text: Ticket sales support the center's sea turtle patients.
experiences.season_text: June and July

experiences.name: Coral nursery snorkel with Coral Restoration Foundation
experiences.description: A restoration talk, then a snorkel trip to a working coral nursery and restoration site off Key Largo with a partner dive shop.
experiences.donation_text: Includes a required $50 donation to Coral Restoration Foundation.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, weather permitting

experiences.description: Permitted guided kayak tour across Kealakekua Bay to snorkel the reef below the monument.

experiences.name: Guided kayak and snorkel to the Captain Cook Monument (Kona Boys)
experiences.description: Permitted guided kayak tour across Kealakekua Bay to snorkel the reef below the monument.

experiences.name: Reef Teach at Kahaluu Bay

experiences.price_text: Free
experiences.season_text: Peak beach hours

experiences.name: Eco sea-scooter snorkel from Kapalua Bay
experiences.description: Guided sea-scooter snorkel along West Maui reefs; guests learn to spot coral bleaching and disease with the Hawaii Coral Institute.

experiences.name: Molokini snorkel eco-tour
experiences.description: Snorkel Molokini with a nonprofit that funds ocean research and education.
experiences.donation_text: Proceeds support Pacific Whale Foundation research and education.
experiences.season_text: Year-round

experiences.name: Hanauma Bay shuttle with guaranteed entry
experiences.description: Round-trip electric shuttle from Waikiki that includes Hanauma Bay admission, so you skip the online reservation scramble.

experiences.name: Guided snorkel at Casino Point
experiences.description: Guided snorkel and gear rental (mask, snorkel, fins, wetsuit) at Avalon's underwater park.

experiences.name: Leopard shark snorkel encounter
experiences.description: Guided snorkel over the sand flats at La Jolla Shores during leopard shark season.
experiences.season_text: From mid-June

experiences.name: La Jolla sea caves kayak and snorkel
experiences.description: Guided kayak along the La Jolla cliffs to the sea caves, with a snorkel stop.

experiences.name: Leopard shark snorkel with Birch Aquarium
experiences.description: Summer snorkel program with Scripps educators to see leopard sharks off La Jolla Shores.
experiences.season_text: Summer

experiences.name: Snorkel and paddle eco-adventure in Biscayne National Park
experiences.description: Six-hour guided trip: snorkel a coral patch reef, wreck or mangrove site chosen by weather, then paddle Jones Lagoon. Bring your own lunch.
experiences.price_text: $209 per person (shared trip)
experiences.season_text: Year-round

experiences.name: Maunalua Bay turtle snorkel by boat
experiences.description: Small-boat snorkel at a reef with daily green sea turtle sightings; flotation and gear included.

experiences.name: Marine biologist guided shore snorkel at Olowalu
experiences.description: Snorkel Maui's oldest reef with a marine biologist: gear, a snorkel lesson, reef-safe sunscreen and photos included.
experiences.price_text: From $119
experiences.season_text: Year-round

experiences.name: Hanauma Bay reef education programme
experiences.description: The required education before you enter, plus the in-park interpretive stations that explain why the reef is recovering here and what visitors do that helps or hurts it.
experiences.price_text: Free with park admission. Non-resident admission is charged separately at the gate.
experiences.donation_text: Proceeds support the park reef monitoring and the native fish restoration ponds.
experiences.season_text: Open daily; the required video can be completed online before you travel.
experiences.meeting_point: Online before your visit, then the park film and reef stations on arrival.

experiences.name: Ahihi-Kinau scenic snorkel and reef interpretation
experiences.description: A snorkel through the Ahihi-Kinau National Historic Landmark with interpretative signs explaining the fish that still shelter in Maui’s clearest natural water, and the shoreline restoration behind it.
experiences.price_text: Free. There is a small parking fee for the landmark.
experiences.donation_text: Admission supports the Ahihi-Kinau shoreline restoration project, which is rebuilding the fish habitat.
experiences.season_text: Best in summer, when the water is calmest and the fish are most active.

experiences.name: Punaluu turtle nesting watch
experiences.description: A quiet evening watch on the black sand at Punaluu, where volunteers record turtle nest locations so the Department of Land and Natural Resources can protect them.
experiences.price_text: Free. Donations cover the volunteer programme.
experiences.donation_text: Donations support turtle nest monitoring and the volunteer teams that move endangered nests to safer sites.
experiences.season_text: Nesting season is roughly April to August, with hatchlings from late July into October.
experiences.meeting_point: Punaluu Black Sand Beach car park.

experiences.name: Maui reef conservation snorkel with a marine biologist
experiences.description: Snorkel the south shore with a Mote Marine Laboratory biologist who records what is on the reef and talks through the difference between a healthy and a degraded Hawaiian reef.
experiences.donation_text: Part of the fee supports ongoing reef monitoring in Maui waters.
experiences.season_text: May to October, when the south shore is calmest.

experiences.name: Coral Restoration Foundation Miami nursery tour
experiences.description: See the nursery lines where staghorn and elkhorn coral are grown from fragments and then outplanted onto Florida’s degraded reef, and find out where the next batch is going.
experiences.donation_text: The nursery programme is funded by donations and by the outplanting trips it runs with volunteers.
experiences.season_text: Tours run on a fixed monthly schedule.

experiences.name: Coral Restoration Foundation Maui coral nursery dive
experiences.description: Help the Coral Restoration Foundation maintain its offshore coral nursery: clean the nursery frames, check the coral for disease and outplant young colonies onto degraded reef.
experiences.donation_text: A portion of the fee supports the nursery and the outplanting programme, which is working to restore the shallow reef that Maui snorkelers see.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, with calmer conditions in the summer.

experiences.name: Kona manta night snorkel with a conservation briefing
experiences.description: Snorkel with the resident manta rays at night after a briefing on why the Hawaiian manta is federally protected and how the photo-identification programme that tracks them works.
experiences.donation_text: Part of the fee supports the operator’s manta monitoring work and the local sighting records that inform protection decisions.
experiences.season_text: Year-round. Manta activity peaks when the water is calm and there is more plankton.

experiences.name: The Reefline guided shore snorkel, Miami Beach
experiences.description: A shore-based guided snorkel over the nearshore reef, run by the team behind The Reefline, with a briefing on how to read reef health and where the restoration outplants are.
experiences.donation_text: Part of the fee goes to nearshore reef monitoring and the local restoration work.
experiences.season_text: Best in the calmer months; mornings year-round.
experiences.meeting_point: Miami Beach shoreline, meeting point confirmed by email.

experiences.name: Biscayne reef and mangrove survey snorkel
experiences.description: Survey the shallow reef and the mangrove edge with Biscayne National Park institute naturalists, logging fish, corals and the condition of the mangrove fringe.
experiences.donation_text: Survey results feed the park’s resource monitoring and are shared with Florida Fish and Wildlife.
experiences.season_text: Best from November to April.

experiences.name: SS Copenhagen historic wreck dive
experiences.description: A dive on the British steamship that wrecked in May 1900 less than a mile offshore, in a state-designated underwater archaeological preserve that protects the wreck exactly as it lies.
experiences.donation_text: Part of the fee supports the preserve and the paperwork that keeps the site protected from salvage.
experiences.season_text: Best in summer, when the visibility is clearest.

experiences.name: Seahorse Valley kayak and snorkel with the Catalina Island Conservancy
experiences.description: Paddle and snorkel the protected waters off the west end of Catalina with the Conservancy, on a route that runs through a marine reserve kept closed to fishing.
experiences.donation_text: Your fee supports the Conservancy’s water quality monitoring, invasive species removal and the island transport that keeps visitor traffic off the reefs.
experiences.season_text: May through October.

experiences.name: Catalina kelp restoration dive
experiences.description: Work with the Catalina Island Conservancy restoring the giant kelp forest: removing urchin holdfasts, transplanting kelp and monitoring how the canopy recovers.
experiences.donation_text: The work protects the kelp forest that the sea lions, fish and shearwaters on the island all depend on.
experiences.season_text: Best from late spring through early autumn when the water is calm.

experiences.name: Scripps Tidewalk with marine scientists
experiences.description: Walk the shallow tide pools with the scientists of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, who identify what is living in the pools and why the water looks the way it does.
experiences.price_text: Free. Registration is required for the tidewalk.
experiences.donation_text: The programme is funded by Scripps and trains the next generation of marine scientists in public outreach.
experiences.season_text: Held on summer weekends around the spring and neap tides.
experiences.meeting_point: Scripps Institution of Oceanography, La Jolla.

experiences.name: Scripps reef survey snorkel
experiences.description: A survey snorkel along the La Jolla reef and kelp forest where the team records species and habitat condition for the long-running Southern California Marine Mammal and Kelp monitoring programme.
experiences.price_text: Free for participants who bring their own snorkel gear.
experiences.donation_text: The survey data supports the kelp forest condition tracking that informs marine protected area management in California.
experiences.season_text: Best from late spring through early autumn, when kelp is at its densest.
experiences.meeting_point: Ellen Browning Scripps Pier, La Jolla.

experiences.name: Florida Keys coral reef survey dive
experiences.description: A citizen-science survey dive on the Keys reef tract, logging species and habitat condition for a monitoring programme that now covers more than a hundred sites from Key Largo to Key West.
experiences.price_text: Free with a donation.
experiences.donation_text: Donations fund the survey coordinator and the open data that researchers and state agencies use.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, with the best conditions in summer.
experiences.meeting_point: Key Largo or Key West marina, depending on the site.

experiences.name: Hawaii reef survey and shoreline cleanup
experiences.description: A volunteer reef survey using the Fish Alert app, paired with a shoreline cleanup at the same beach. Divers and snorkelers log what they see; the data goes to a long-running coral reef monitoring programme.
experiences.price_text: Free. Gear and a data briefing are provided.
experiences.donation_text: Your survey data goes into the Coral Reef Evaluation and Monitoring Project, and your cleanup hours count towards shoreline stewardship.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, with surveys scheduled around the calmer months.
experiences.meeting_point: Meeting point depends on the beach; details are sent with the confirmation.

experiences.name: REEF Hawaii coral reef survey dive
experiences.description: A guided reef survey where every fish is logged to species. The data feeds the largest citizen-science coral reef monitoring programme in the world and is published openly.
experiences.price_text: Free with a donation to the programme.
experiences.donation_text: Donations fund the survey coordination and the open data platform that universities use.
experiences.season_text: Year-round; the water is clearest in summer.

experiences.name: Guided snorkel of the Shipwreck Snorkel Trail
experiences.description: A guided swim along the 2002 trail laid over the SS Copenhagen, with a guide who explains what each piece of the wreck was and how the site was dedicated in 2002.
experiences.price_text: Free with a donation to the Marine Archaeological Council.
experiences.donation_text: Donations pay for mooring buoys, marker maintenance and the educational panels on the trail.
experiences.season_text: Best on a calm day; the markers are hard to find in a swell.

experiences.name: Lauderdale reef health survey snorkel
experiences.description: Log the fish and coral on the three-tier reef and on the shipwreck trail, so the Marine Archaeological Council can track how the artificial reef and the natural reef beside it change over time.
experiences.price_text: Free with a donation.
experiences.donation_text: Donations fund the survey equipment and the annual reef health report for the town.
experiences.season_text: Year-round on calm days.

experiences.name: Florida Keys Maritime Heritage Trail snorkel
experiences.description: Snorkel the sanctuary’s Maritime Heritage Trail, where markers point out the Old Seven Mile Bridge, the wrecks of the 1912 Overseas Railway and the shipwrecks that took Florida’s first underwater preserve.
experiences.donation_text: The trail is maintained by the sanctuary and the dive and snorkel community that adopts its markers.
experiences.season_text: Best from May to October.
experiences.meeting_point: Marathon, or the Key West docks for the southern sections.

experiences.name: Dry Tortugas reef and fort interpretation
experiences.description: A ranger-led programme at Fort Jefferson covering the island history, the shipwrecks on the reef, and how the third-largest barrier reef on the planet is protected and why the rules matter.
experiences.price_text: Free with park admission.
experiences.donation_text: Park admission funds the rangers, the fort preservation and the mooring buoy system.
experiences.season_text: Year-round; the programme is best booked on a calm day.
experiences.meeting_point: Fort Jefferson visitor area, Dry Tortugas.

experiences.name: Broward County coral reef restoration outplant
experiences.description: Join a Florida Department of Environmental Protection dive team as they reattach and re-cement staghorn coral fragments onto the nearshore reef, including the reef in front of Lauderdale-by-the-Sea.
experiences.donation_text: The outplanting programme is funded by state restoration money and by the volunteers who do the work.
experiences.season_text: Best from June to October, when the water is calmest and the coral is not in a growth flush.
experiences.group_size_text: Limited to 10 divers or snorkelers per trip.

experiences.name: Springs wildlife viewing and education area
experiences.description: The state’s wildlife viewing area on the Manatee Springs run, with an interpretive kiosk explaining why cold spring water and a warm winter combine to draw so much wildlife to one place.
experiences.price_text: Free with park admission.
experiences.donation_text: Admission supports the viewing area, the river boardwalks and the spring water flow monitoring.
experiences.season_text: Best in the cooler months, when manatees gather in the numbers.
experiences.meeting_point: Manatee Springs State Park, wildlife viewing area.

experiences.name: Gilchrist Blue Springs wild river walk
experiences.description: A short guided walk along the spring run and out to the Santa Fe River, where a state interpreter explains how the aquifer works and why the colour of the water changes with the season.
experiences.price_text: Free with park admission.
experiences.donation_text: Admission supports the wild river boardwalk and the spring flow monitoring programme.
experiences.season_text: Year-round.

experiences.name: Broward County beach turtle nesting walk
experiences.description: Walk a nesting beach at dusk with a Florida Fish and Wildlife conservation volunteer who marks nests, checks for strandings and explains how lighting and beach development affect loggerhead and green turtles.
experiences.price_text: Free. Registration is required.
experiences.donation_text: The programme is funded by the state and by volunteers who monitor more than a hundred miles of nesting beach each summer.
experiences.season_text: Nesting season runs from March to October, with hatchlings from July to October.
experiences.meeting_point: Beach access varies; the meeting point is confirmed by email.

experiences.name: Florida Keys loggerhead nesting walk
experiences.description: A dusk walk on a Keys nesting beach with a state sea turtle biologist, covering why the Keys still hold one of the last large loggerhead nesting aggregations in the western Atlantic.
experiences.price_text: Free. Registration is required.
experiences.donation_text: The programme is funded by the state and supports nest monitoring and the volunteer rescue hotline.
experiences.season_text: Nesting from March to October, hatchlings from July to October.
experiences.meeting_point: Meeting point confirmed by email after registration.

experiences.name: Spring bass catch and release clinic
experiences.description: Learn to fish for Florida largemouth bass in cold spring water with a state biologist, then release the fish straight back. Tackle, bait and licences are provided.
experiences.price_text: Free. A valid Florida fishing licence is required and can be bought on the day.
experiences.donation_text: Free licence waivers for veterans and for participants under 16.
experiences.season_text: Best from October to April, when the bass are concentrated in the spring runs.

experiences.name: Wild manatee watch at Manatee Springs
experiences.description: A quiet, guide-led watch from the boardwalk and the water for the wild manatees that gather in the cool spring run, with the rules for respectful distance explained before you enter.
experiences.price_text: Free with park admission.
experiences.donation_text: Admission supports the manatee viewing area and the state manatee rescue programme.
experiences.season_text: Best from November to March.

experiences.name: Sunset Cliffs and Ocean Beach coastal cleanup
experiences.description: Join Surfrider Foundation San Diego on the same stretch of coast where the kelp forest is recovering, clearing marine debris and logging what washes ashore.
experiences.price_text: Free. Gloves, bags and grabbers are provided.
experiences.donation_text: The data from each cleanup goes into the Surfrider chapters national database, and the litter is sorted for recycling.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, with the biggest shoreline cleanups in spring and autumn.
experiences.meeting_point: Sunset Cliffs Boulevard, meeting point confirmed by email.

experiences.name: John Pennekamp glass-bottom boat
experiences.description: The park’s 65-foot glass-bottom catamaran, with a maximum of 130 passengers, running over the shallow reef and the drop-off with a naturalist on the microphone.
experiences.price_text: Around $30-35 per adult, and less for children. Tour prices are set by the park and change.
experiences.donation_text: A share of the tour price goes back into the park’s reef monitoring and education programmes.
experiences.season_text: Year-round, with the clearest water in summer.
experiences.meeting_point: John Pennekamp State Park, Key Largo.

experiences.name: Kayak the spring runs
experiences.description: Paddle the spring runs and the Santa Fe River, which is how most people first see the clear blue water and the spring vents from above.
experiences.season_text: Best from October to April.

experiences.name: Hawaii Wildlife Center sea turtle release
experiences.description: Watch the Hawaii Wildlife Center release rehabilitated green sea turtles back into the ocean, and learn what makes a turtle healthy versus stressed on the beach.
experiences.price_text: Free to watch. Donations support the hospital and the rescue work.
experiences.donation_text: Donations go to the turtle hospital, the ambulance service and the beach rescue programme.
experiences.season_text: Release days are announced through the centre, generally in the morning.

faqs.question: Do you need a reservation for Hanauma Bay?
faqs.answer: Yes, if you are not a Hawaii resident. Reservations open online two days ahead at 7:00 a.m. HST. Hawaii residents with ID enter free without one.

faqs.question: How much does Hanauma Bay cost?
faqs.answer: $25 per non-resident aged 13 and over, plus a 2.35% online fee. Children 12 and under are free. Parking is $3 for non-residents.

faqs.question: What days is Hanauma Bay closed?
faqs.answer: Every Monday and Tuesday, plus Christmas Day and New Year's Day. The closures give the reef time to recover.

faqs.question: Can you see turtles at Hanauma Bay?
faqs.answer: Often. Green sea turtles feed in the bay, and Hawaiian monk seals haul out on the beach in spring and summer. Keep your distance from both.

faqs.question: Is Hanauma Bay good for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes. The inner reef is shallow and sheltered, and you can rent gear on site. Leave the outer bay to experienced swimmers.

faqs.question: Is Two Step good for beginners?
faqs.answer: It suits confident swimmers better than first-timers. Boat traffic at the ramp; careful entry and exit on the lava ledges.

faqs.question: Is Kahaluu Beach Park good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is the Kona manta site good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Waialea Bay good for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is one of the easier spots in the area.

faqs.question: Is Molokini Crater good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Honolua Bay good for beginners?
faqs.answer: It suits confident swimmers better than first-timers. Rocky entry; check for surf before going in.

faqs.question: Is Black Rock good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Kapalua Bay good for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is one of the easier spots in the area.

faqs.question: Is Olowalu Reef good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Ahihi-Kinau Natural Area Reserve good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Maluaka Beach good for beginners?
faqs.answer: Yes, it is one of the easier spots in the area.

faqs.question: Is Sharks Cove good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Kuilima Cove good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Lovers Cove good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Casino Point Dive Park good for beginners?

faqs.question: Is Descanso Beach good for beginners?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Kuilima Cove?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Sharks Cove?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Lovers Cove?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel La Jolla Shores?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel La Jolla Cove?

faqs.question: Why is Fanning Springs so dangerous?
faqs.answer: The current. A huge volume of water leaves the spring bowl and accelerates down the river, and swimming against it is exhausting. Stay in the river run, keep off the spring head, and use a float if you are not a strong swimmer.

faqs.question: Can I see manatees at the springs?
faqs.answer: Often, in the cooler months. Manatee Springs and Fanning Springs are the reliable ones, from roughly November to March, when the water is cold enough for them but warm enough for Florida.

faqs.question: Is swimming at Rainbow Springs worth the entrance fee?
faqs.answer: Yes. The head spring pool is 5 to 18 ft deep and the 400-foot cave beside it is a genuine attraction, though the cave itself is closed to swimmers. You pay $8 per vehicle or $6 per person on foot or by bike.

faqs.question: How cold is the water in the Florida Springs?
faqs.answer: Remarkably stable. The spring water is about 68 to 72 degrees all year, because it comes from the Floridan aquifer and never sees sunlight. That makes the springs far more comfortable than the ocean in summer.

faqs.question: Can I snorkel with manatees in South Florida?
faqs.answer: Yes, in the spring runs rather than the sea. Manatee Springs and Fanning Springs give the best odds in the cooler months, from about November to March.

faqs.question: When is the water clearest in South Florida?
faqs.answer: Late spring through early autumn, when the water is warmest and there is less wind. Winter water is clearer but colder, and the Florida Springs are at their most attractive then.

faqs.question: Do I need a boat to snorkel in South Florida?
faqs.answer: Not always. Biscayne National Park, Crandon Park and the Datura Avenue beach portal are all shore entries. John Pennekamp, Dry Tortugas and Sand Key are boat-only, because the reef there is 3 to 8 miles offshore.

faqs.question: Which part of South Florida is best for a first snorkel?
faqs.answer: Biscayne National Park and the nearshore reef off Crandon Park are the gentlest, with a shallow sandy bottom and no current. The Lauderdale reef and the Keys are the best once you are comfortable in open water.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get to the Dry Tortugas?
faqs.answer: About two hours by ferry from Key West, or a similar run by boat from Marathon or Key Largo. Allow a full day, carry water, and expect no freshwater and almost no shade on the island.

faqs.question: Can you snorkel with turtles in the Florida Keys?
faqs.answer: Yes, though it is not guaranteed. Loggerheads nest on the Keys beaches and hawksbills still nest in small numbers. Keep at least 10 ft away and never block a turtle heading for the surface.

faqs.question: Do I need a dive flag in the Florida Keys?
faqs.answer: Yes. Florida law requires a dive flag for snorkelers and divers in state waters, and John Pennekamp and Dry Tortugas both enforce it. If you are on a tour, the boat provides one.

faqs.question: What is the best snorkeling spot in the Florida Keys?
faqs.answer: For snorkelers, John Pennekamp State Park is the benchmark: the reef starts right at the sand and the shallow top is snorkelable from the beach or the glass-bottom boat. The Dry Tortugas have the best drop-offs and the biggest species list.

faqs.question: Is there a lifeguard at the Lauderdale beach?
faqs.answer: No. Lauderdale-by-the-Sea is a street-access beach without lifeguards, and boat traffic is heavy. Stay clear of the pier and the marked channel.

faqs.question: Can I snorkel the SS Copenhagen?
faqs.answer: Not really. The top of the wreck is in about 25 ft of water, well past snorkel depth. It is a dive site inside a Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve, where touching or removing anything is prohibited.

faqs.question: Is the Shipwreck Snorkel Trail hard to find?
faqs.answer: Moderately. The markers are small pairs of yellow buoys and they are easy to miss from the surface, so ask locally or go with a guided tour from the Marine Archaeological Council. Swim in from the Datura Avenue portal.

faqs.question: How do you get to the Datura Avenue reef?
faqs.answer: Drive to Datura Avenue at El Mar Drive and walk through the beach portal at the end of the street. The reef starts about 100 yards offshore and the water is waist to chest deep on it.

faqs.answer: Yes. John Pennekamp State Park is only reachable by boat, so you need a tour or charter. On US 1 in Key Largo, about 60 miles north of Key West and 25 miles south of Marathon.

faqs.question: Do you need a tour to snorkel Dry Tortugas National Park?
faqs.answer: Yes. Dry Tortugas National Park is only reachable by boat, so you need a tour or charter. Ferry from Key West, or a boat from Key West, Marathon or Key Largo.

faqs.question: Do you need a tour to snorkel Old Seven Mile Bridge Piles?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. On US 1 in Marathon, at the west end of the Old Seven Mile Bridge, at the historic bridge parking area.

faqs.question: Do you need a tour to snorkel Sand Key Lighthouse?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sand Key Lighthouse is only reachable by boat, so you need a tour or charter. Water taxi or private boat from Key West, about eight miles out.

faqs.question: Do you need a tour to snorkel SS Copenhagen?

faqs.question: Do you need a tour to snorkel Crandon Park?
faqs.answer: No. You can snorkel Crandon Park on your own from the shore. None.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Makena Beach?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Wailea Beach?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Lanikai Beach?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Sunset Cliffs Marine Reserve?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Rainbow Springs State Park?
faqs.answer: $8 per vehicle, or $6 per person if you enter on foot or by bike. Parking: Parking at the park entrance. A boardwalk runs to the head spring pool.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Gilchrist Blue Springs?
faqs.answer: Free. There is no entrance fee and no parking fee. Parking: Free gravel parking lot beside the spring.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Fanning Springs State Park?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Manatee Springs State Park?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel John Pennekamp State Park?
faqs.answer: Free to enter the park. The glass-bottom boat is priced separately, at roughly $30-35 per adult. Parking: Park parking is free and fills early at weekends.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Dry Tortugas National Park?
faqs.answer: The park entrance fee is $15 per person; children under 16 enter free. Boat passage is extra and varies by operator. Parking: There is no parking on the island. Everything comes in by ferry or boat.

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Old Seven Mile Bridge Piles?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Sand Key Lighthouse?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel SS Copenhagen?

faqs.question: How much does it cost to snorkel Crandon Park?
